name: Local Phase Analysis
description: Analyzes local phase information in frequency domain for tampering detection — phase consistency violations indicate manipulation (Oppenheim & Lim, 1981).
mechanism:
This method analyzes the phase spectrum of local image regions to detect manipulations and AI-generated content, exploiting the fact that phase carries most structural information:

1. **Local Phase Spectrum Extraction**: The image is divided into overlapping patches (typically 64×64 or 128×128). For each patch, the 2D DFT is computed, yielding magnitude |F(u,v)| and phase φ(u,v) = arctan(Im(F)/Re(F)). Phase encodes the positions and shapes of structures (Oppenheim & Lim, 1981), while magnitude encodes contrast. The method focuses on phase because it is more sensitive to manipulation artifacts than magnitude.

2. **Phase Coherence Analysis**: In natural images, phase relationships across adjacent patches exhibit smooth spatial variation governed by scene geometry. The method computes phase coherence C(u,v) = |Σ exp(jφ_k(u,v))| / N across N neighboring patches for each frequency component (u,v). High coherence indicates consistent phase relationships; low coherence at specific frequencies indicates manipulation boundaries where phase continuity is broken by splicing or inpainting.

3. **Phase Congruency Mapping**: Following Kovesi's framework, phase congruency PC(x) = Σ_n W_n(x) × |A_n(x) cos(φ_n(x) − φ̄(x)) − T| / (Σ_n A_n(x) + ε) is computed using Log-Gabor filters at multiple scales and orientations. Phase congruency provides an illumination-invariant and contrast-invariant measure of structural significance. In manipulated regions, phase congruency patterns differ from authentic regions due to inconsistencies in the underlying signal structure.

4. **Cross-Patch Phase Residual**: For each frequency band, the method computes the phase residual Δφ between each patch and its spatial prediction (bilinear interpolation from neighboring patches). In unmanipulated images, |Δφ| follows a von Mises distribution with small concentration parameter κ. Manipulation introduces phase discontinuities that appear as outliers in this distribution, detectable using a likelihood ratio test.
parameters:
Patch size: 64×64 or 128×128 pixels
Patch overlap: 75%
Log-Gabor scales: 4
Log-Gabor orientations: 6
Phase coherence neighborhood: 5×5 patches
Von Mises outlier threshold: κ > 3.0
Minimum image size: 128×128 pixels
accuracy: 81–89% accuracy for splicing detection using phase coherence features. Phase congruency achieves AUC of 0.87 for manipulation localization. Cross-patch phase residual detects AI-inpainted regions with F1-score of 0.85. Phase-based features are robust to JPEG compression down to quality factor 60.
source: Oppenheim, A. V. & Lim, J. S. (1981). The Importance of Phase in Signals. Proceedings of the IEEE, 69(5), 529–541.
useCase: Detecting spliced regions through phase coherence violations. Localizing AI-inpainted regions with inconsistent phase structure. Illumination-invariant manipulation detection using phase congruency. Identifying copy-move forgeries through phase residual analysis.
strengths:
• Phase carries more structural information than magnitude spectrum
• Phase coherence is robust to global illumination and contrast changes
• Detects subtle manipulations invisible to spatial-domain methods
• Phase congruency provides contrast-invariant edge/feature detection
• Multiple complementary phase features reduce false positive rate
limitations:
• Phase analysis requires sufficient image resolution (> 128×128 pixels)
• Heavily blurred or out-of-focus regions have weak phase structure
• Phase wrapping artifacts at ±π require careful unwrapping algorithms
• Periodic textures (e.g., bricks, fabric) produce strong phase patterns that may confuse analysis
• Computational cost is higher than spatial-domain methods due to FFT per patch

references.title: Oppenheim, A. V. & Lim, J. S. — The Importance of Phase in Signals (1981)
Kovesi, P. — Image Features from Phase Congruency (1999)
